subject: wood turtle
title: This Turtle Stomps the Ground and Earthworms Come Up to Be Eaten

scenes.text: A turtle stomps the ground, and worms come up to it.
The wood turtle rocks side to side, stamping its front feet. Left, right, left.
A naturalist watched one do it for half an hour, snatching earthworms as they surfaced.
But why would a worm crawl up to a predator?
In 2008 a biologist tested it. Worms bolt for the surface when they feel a digging mole, their worst enemy.
So the worm flees a mole that isn't there, straight into a turtle. Gulls do the same dance.

description:
A turtle stomps the ground, and earthworms come up to be eaten.
Naturalist John Kaufmann described wood turtles rocking as they stomped with their front feet, alternating left and right, for half an hour at a time, and snatching the earthworms that surfaced. Gulls paddle their feet to the same effect, and people in Florida's Apalachicola National Forest do it for bait by rubbing a wooden stake with a steel rooping iron. In 2008, Vanderbilt biologist Kenneth Catania showed why it works: the vibrations resemble those of a burrowing mole, and worms escape moles by fleeing to the surface, an idea Charles Darwin had already recorded. Rain, the older explanation, brought up almost no worms in his tests.
Would you have guessed the mole? Comment below.
first_comment: Human worm grunters in Florida can bring up thousands of worms in a day with a wooden stake and a strip of steel. Would you have guessed the mole?
